The Uncertainty of a Predicted Predictor

Source: R/predict.R
predict_se.Rd

Computes the standard error of each equation's linear predictor, and of the parameter that the predictor gives, with an interval.

Usage

predict_se(object, spec, design, ep, level = 0.95, ...)

Arguments

object

A fitted model.

spec

The specification the prediction is made under.

design

Its design.

ep

The predictors and parameters, as statmod_eta() returns them.

level

The interval's level.

...

Passed to vcov(), which also receives readable = FALSE from this function.

Value

A named list, one entry per distribution parameter, each a data frame with the columns eta, se_eta, eta_lower and eta_upper on the link scale and fit, se, lower and upper on the parameter scale.

The delta method, equation by equation

An equation's predictor is \(\eta_{ip} = x_{ip}'\beta_p\), so its variance is \(x_{ip}' V_{pp} x_{ip}\), with \(V\) the variance of the coefficients as estimated: the coordinates, since the design is written in them, not the quantities that coef.StatmodFit() reports by default.

The equations do not mix. One equation's predictor reads only the coefficients of that equation, whatever the covariance between the blocks. A predictor that reads no coefficient (an equation written as ~ 0, or an equation with only an offset) is a known constant, with a standard error of zero.

A term whose block moves needs no special case

Its block is the Jacobian \(\partial\eta/\partial\beta\) by construction, which is why a linear fit on it is a Gauss-Newton step. The row is therefore already the derivative, and the delta method is exact to first order. That covers modelterms7::seg(), modelterms7::nl() and a smoothed modelterms7::jump() or modelterms7::jseg(), including the parameters of a nonlinear term developed over covariates. A sharp modelterms7::jump() or modelterms7::jseg() is fitted as an ordinary block at its settled break-point, so the standard error of a prediction that reads it is finite and is conditional on that position.

The interval

The interval is built on the scale on which the equation is written and mapped back through the link, as every interval in this toolkit is. A scale parameter under a log link, for example, cannot have a negative lower end.

A coefficient with no variance carries none forward

An entry of the variance that is not finite blanks the standard error of the rows whose design reaches it, and does not blank that of any other row. An aliased coefficient is such a case. The position of a sharp break-point term is held and has no variance either, but its column of the design is zero, so it blanks no row.

A coefficient that a lasso, an elastic net, a SCAD or an MCP holds at exactly zero is treated as fixed: the model is selected without it, its row of the variance is NA, and its column of the design is left out of the quadratic form, so it contributes nothing. Otherwise a prediction at new data would read every such coefficient against a non-zero covariate and return NA on every row.

See also

predict.StatmodFit(), vcov.StatmodFit()
